deep.reconstruction:
This page continues Euler's chapter on biquadratic (quartic) residues modulo a prime p = 4q+1. From the previous page, a is a quartic residue iff a^q ≡ 1 (mod p). Also −1 is a quartic residue iff q is even, i.e. iff p ≡ 1 (mod 8).

§455. If p ≡ 5 (mod 8) (5, 13, 29, 37, 53, 61, 101, …), then q is odd. So −1 is not a quartic residue, and p cannot divide a^4+b^4 when p∤ab: otherwise (a/b)^4 ≡ −1. A prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) does not even divide a^2+b^2 with p∤ab, because −1 is a quadratic non-residue. (Implicit, mine: one needs p∤a, p∤b; Euler adds the coprimality hypothesis in §456.)

§456. Conclusion: for gcd(a,b)=1, every prime divisor of a^4+b^4 other than 2 is ≡ 1 (mod 8). Euler gives a table of a^4+b^4 for all coprime pairs 1 ≤ a < b ≤ 10, with factorizations. Every odd factor shown is ≡ 1 (mod 8): 17, 41, 73, 89, 97, 113, 137, 193, 241, 257, 313, 337, 353, 401, 593, 641, …

§457. When is 2 a quartic residue mod p? Euler notes it never happens in the small cases worked out in §424. If 2 ≡ x^4 then, multiplying by residues, 2b^4 ≡ a^4. So p divides some a^4 − 2b^4 (or 2b^4 − a^4). Factoring such numbers yields the primes 73, 89, 113, 233, 281, 353, 593, 617, 937, 1249, 1889, 2273, 2393, 4177, 4721, 4801, 6529. Euler conjectures that these are exactly the primes of the form 64y^2 + x^2.

§458. He lists the primes x^2 + 64y^2 up to 1249: 73, 89, 113, 233, 257, 281, 337, 353, 577, 593, 601, 617, 881, 937, 1033, 1049, 1097, 1153, 1193, 1201, 1249. He says that all the earlier primes occur here, and that the others also satisfy the requirement, which he presumably checked. Hence he trusts the conjecture. Since all these primes are ≡ 1 (mod 8), −1 is a quartic residue, so −2 is one as well.

§459. Empirically, for every prime p = 4q+1 ≤ 101, q is a quartic residue: q^q ≡ 1 (mod p). If true in general, then the following are also residues, since 16, 81, 256 are fourth powers and residues are closed under products:
- q, q^2, q^3, 16q, 81q, 256q, 16q^2, 81q^2;
- hence, using 4q ≡ −1: 16q ≡ −4, 81q = q + 80q ≡ q − 20, 256q ≡ −64, and 16q^2 ≡ 1 ≡ −4q.

§460 (begins). This is linked to §389: 2 is a quadratic residue for p ≡ 1 (mod 8) and a non-residue for p ≡ 5 (mod 8). On the next page Euler deduces that 4^q ≡ ±1 accordingly, so (−4)^q ≡ 1 in both cases. Thus −4, and hence q ≡ −1/4, is always a quartic residue, which proves the §459 observation. Modern view: −4 = (1+i)^4, and i exists mod p.

Footnote (marginal note). For 3 to be a quartic residue, p = x^2 + y^2 must have either x = 12m, or x = 3(2m+1) with y = 4n+2. For 5 to be a quartic residue, p = 100x^2 + y^2.
errors: Table entry 3^4+10^4: printed '= 2.17.593', but 81+10000 = 10081 = 17·593 is odd (3 and 10 have opposite parity). The factor 2 is spurious.
Table entry 9^4+10^4: printed '= 16511', but 6561+10000 = 16561, which is prime (≡ 1 mod 8). The printed 16511 = 11·19·79 would contradict the theorem just stated.
§458 list of primes x^2+64y^2 up to 1249 omits 1217 = 31^2 + 64·2^2, which is prime and ≡ 1 mod 8.
§455 tacitly needs p∤ab (gcd(a,b)=1); Euler supplies this in §456.
§459 is presented only as an induction from p ≤ 101. It is in fact always true, as Euler shows on the next page via −4 being a quartic residue.
In §459 the derived residue '−4q' is trivial, since −4q ≡ 1 mod p. The 81qq ≡ 81/16 entry is not reduced further.

results.what: For gcd(a,b)=1, odd prime divisors of a^4+b^4 are ≡ 1 (mod 8); primes ≡ 5 (mod 8) and ≡ 3 (mod 4) never divide a^4+b^4
results.modern_name: −1 is a quartic residue mod p iff p ≡ 1 (mod 8); prime divisors of x^4+y^4

results.what: Table of factorizations of a^4+b^4 for coprime a<b≤10
Conjecture: 2 is a biquadratic residue mod prime p iff p = x^2 + 64y^2
results.usually_credited_to: Conjectured by Euler (Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, publ. 1849); proved by Gauss (Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum I, 1828); elementary proofs by Dirichlet

results.what: For p = 4q+1, q (equivalently −4) is always a quartic residue
results.modern_name: −4 = (1+i)^4 is a fourth power mod p ≡ 1 (mod 4)

results.what: Marginal conjectures: 3 is a quartic residue iff p = x^2+y^2 with x ≡ 0 (mod 12), or x an odd multiple of 3 and y ≡ 2 (mod 4); 5 is a quartic residue iff p = x^2+100y^2
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjecture, Tractatus); proofs by Gauss/Lebesgue/Dirichlet era

deep.surprise_reason: The x^2+64y^2 conjecture for the quartic character of 2, and the marginal conjectures for 3 and 5, are well documented as Euler's from the Tractatus (e.g. Cox, Lemmermeyer). The rest is routine or already in Euler's published work.

checkable.asserts: 9^4+10^4 = 16561 is a prime ≡ 1 mod 8 (printed 16511 is wrong)
The printed value 16511 would violate the theorem

checkable.sympy: all(all(p == 2 or p % 8 == 1 for p in primefactors(a**4+b**4)) for a in range(1,11) for b in range(a+1,11) if gcd(a,b) == 1)
checkable.asserts: Theorem of §456 holds on the whole table

checkable.sympy: [p for p in primerange(3,1300) if p % 8 == 1 and pow(2,(p-1)//4,p) == 1] == [p for p in primerange(3,1300) if any(p - 64*y**2 > 0 and sqrt(p - 64*y**2).is_integer for y in range(1,5))]
checkable.asserts: Euler/Gauss: 2 is a quartic residue iff p = x^2+64y^2 (checked up to 1300; includes 1217)
Every prime in Euler's §457 list has 2 as a quartic residue

checkable.sympy: all(pow((p-1)//4, (p-1)//4, p) == 1 for p in primerange(5,2000) if p % 4 == 1)
checkable.asserts: §459: q is a quartic residue mod p = 4q+1 (true in general)

checkable.sympy: all(pow(-4 % p, (p-1)//4, p) == 1 for p in primerange(5,2000) if p % 4 == 1)
checkable.asserts: −4 is always a quartic residue mod p ≡ 1 mod 4

checkable.sympy: all((pow(5,(p-1)//4,p) == 1) == any(p - 100*y**2 > 0 and sqrt(p - 100*y**2).is_integer for y in range(1,10)) for p in primerange(3,5000) if p % 4 == 1)
checkable.asserts: Marginal note: 5 is a quartic residue iff p = x^2+100y^2
1217 is a prime of form x^2+64y^2 omitted from the §458 list

transcription_corrections: Footer reads 'L. Euleri Op. posthuma. T. I.' (not 'postuma').
The table is set in four columns; the transcription's row order mixes the columns but the entries match the image.
Entry '6^4+7^4 = 3697' is correct (the print shows a damaged '6').
'3^4+10^4 = 2.17.593' and '9^4+10^4 = 16511.' faithfully reproduce the printed page but are arithmetic errors in the original (should be 17·593 and 16561).
